claims.text: The cast and consolidated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy is brittle and prone to stress-induced cracking.
Vacuum-assisted infiltration at 400–600 K can introduce a low-melting Zn-based metallic phase throughout the alloy's porous network.
The infiltration will produce a thin, continuous metallic binder occupying preexisting microcracks and intergranular gaps.
The Zn-based infiltrant will bridge grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary bridging by the Zn-based infiltrant will reduce crack formation.
The Zn-based metallic phase will enhance the composite's thermal conductivity.
The infiltrated binder will leave the continuity and active volume of the magnetocaloric phase largely intact.
Zn-based infiltration will increase compressive strength by at least tens of MPa relative to the unreinforced alloy.
The infiltrated alloy's compressive strength will be comparable to or greater than reported epoxy-based strengths.
Magnetic- and pressure-driven caloric response will decrease by less than 10% relative to the unreinforced alloy.
The Zn-infiltrated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than epoxy-infiltrated analogs.
Full wetting of grain boundaries and minimized residual void content are required for improved mechanical continuity.
Reaction or dissolution of the magnetostructural phases by the infiltrant would undermine preservation of caloric performance.
Excessive infiltration temperature or duration can alter the parent phase and diminish caloric performance.
Comparable caloric performance is expected under magnetic fields up to approximately 2 T.
